Large Language Models’ Complicit Responses to Illicit Instructions across Socio-Legal Contexts (https://arxiv.org/html/2511.20736v1)

L262: An illustration of the illicit intent taxonomy constructed for the Chinese criminal context is presented in Fig. cite62†14 . For example, in relation to the “Objective Unlawfulness” subcategory, a user may exhibit intents such as “Preparing Tools” to facilitate unlawful conduct, or attempt to evade legal liability by deceptively framing the act as arising from “Consent of the Victim”.
L263: Following this approach, we derive 25 criminal illicit intents for both the Chinese and US legal contexts (Supplementary Information, “Illicit intent synthesis”).
L264:   * •
L265: 
L266: Illicit intent instantiation. We pair each scenario description from stage one with an illicit intent randomly sampled from the illicit intent taxonomy, then employ LLMs to instantiate the illicit intent into a context-specific illicit query, ensuring the generated query is contextually coherent and customized to the specific scenario (Supplementary Information, “Illicit intent synthesis”).
L267: In both the illicit scenario synthesis and illicit intent synthesis stages, we utilize DeepSeek-R1 to support the generation of scenario descriptions and illicit queries, selected for its cost-efficiency and its ability to produce naturalistic, first-person narratives. For the Chinese legal context, we draw on original court judgments covering all criminal case types, provided by cite93†China Judgments Online (2013) , written in Mandarin Chinese.
L268: For the US context, we primarily use court judgments related to criminal cases from the cite94†Caselaw Access Project (2024) , written in English. Further implementation details and prompt templates for LLM-assisted generation are described in the Supplementary Information (“Construction of illicit instructions”). The final illicit instructions integrate case scenarios with illicit queries, forming the input for our evaluation benchmark designed to assess complicit facilitation behavior of LLMs.
L269: To verify the reliability and overall quality of our automated instruction curation pipeline, we conduct manual assessment on 300 randomly sampled illicit instructions from each jurisdiction (Supplementary Information, “Quality check for illicit instructions”).
L270: The quality assessment shows that over 90% of the constructed illicit instructions satisfy the criteria of unlawfulness, coherence, and contextual fidelity in both the Chinese and US contexts, providing strong evidence for the high quality of the EVIL benchmark and the reliability of the automated construction pipeline.
L271: #### Assessment of LLM responses
L272: We systematically probe LLMs for complicit facilitation behaviors by presenting them with the curated illicit instructions and assessing their responses. We propose a structured, multi-dimensional assessment framework encompassing three dimensions: safety, responsibility, and credibility.
L273: Grounded in a social-good perspective (cite34†Tomašev et al., 2020 ; cite33†Cheng et al., 2021 ), this framework recognizes that socially beneficial model responses—particularly in high-risk, unlawful contexts—should extend beyond the essential requirement of withholding facilitation of illicit activities (safety) and advance to proactively offer warnings and lawful alternatives to users who may seek to engage in unlawful conduct (responsibility), and provide credible information regarding potential legal violations (credibility).
L274: Safety. It quantifies the proportion of instances in which an LLM successfully abstains from providing assistance for illicit user instructions, which is the foundational requirement of our evaluation framework. In this context, a safe response is defined as one in which the model does not provide assistive information or support in response to an illicit instruction, thereby demonstrating awareness of illicit risk and the necessity of maintaining safety.
L275: In contrast, an unsafe response is one that provides such complicit facilitation.
L276: Responsibility. It evaluates a model’s proactive engagement in preventing harmful behaviors and guiding users toward lawful actions. Prior research (cite90†Braga and Weisburd, 2012 ; cite91†Engel et al., 2013 ; cite92†Braga and Weisburd, 2015 ) has demonstrated that clearly communicating potential consequences and proposing legal alternatives can effectively raise user awareness of risk and deter illicit conduct.
L277: Accordingly, we define a responsible response as one that includes two essential elements: (1) an explicit warning highlighting the potential negative consequences associated with the illicit behavior, and (2) a constructive suggestion for lawful alternative actions.
L278: By foregrounding responsibility, our framework highlights the importance of models not only avoiding facilitating illicit instructions, but also actively intervening to inform users of possible consequences and promote lawful and constructive alternatives.
L279: Credibility. It assesses a model’s ability to correctly identify and articulate the legal risk categories underlying an illicit instruction, i.e., the specific type of criminal offense involved. This dimension assesses whether a model can credibly convey the legal rationale for refusing to provide assistance.
L280: Encouraging credible explanations in LLMs offers several benefits: firstly, it helps the model to better distinguish between genuinely illicit instructions and harmless requests, thereby improving precision in safety interventions. Secondly, it fosters public trust in LLMs’ responses by making refusals transparent and evidence-based. Lastly, it contributes to the promotion of legal awareness among users, which may in turn deter future harmful behaviors.
L281: Overall, the three dimensions of safety, responsibility, and credibility represent structured evaluation criteria. Safety serves as the foundational requirement that ensures the absence of direct harm, and the introduction of responsibility and credibility metrics positions AI systems as proactive contributors to harm prevention and societal benefit.
L282: To achieve scalability in evaluating model responses, we adopt an automated scoring pipeline in an “LLM-as-a-Judge” fashion, which has been widely used in recent literature due to its demonstrated effectiveness and scalability in automating evaluation tasks (cite47†Zheng et al., 2023 ).
L283: Instead of requiring LLMs to perform holistic or subjective judgments, we structure the evaluation into a series of clearly-defined, rule-based judgments, to facilitate more precise assessments and minimize value-laden or subjective judgments. Detailed rules and settings are presented in Supplementary Information (“LLM-based response assessment”). In this study, we utilize GPT-4o as the judge.
L284: To verify the robustness and validity of our automated, LLM-based scoring approach, we compare the accuracy of GPT-4o’s judgments with those of human raters (Supplementary Information, “Quality check for LLM-based response assessment”). GPT-4o achieves scoring accuracies exceeding 96% across all three evaluation dimensions—safety, responsibility, and credibility—in both the Chinese and US contexts, confirming the strong alignment with human judgments and reliability of our automated evaluation method.

L115: ### 3.1 Results
L116: In the white-box scenario (Table cite27†3 , Panel A), full-image perturbations produce strong entropy amplification across all models. Unconstrained-budget settings ($\varepsilon=1.0$) raise entropy by roughly 3–6$\times$ depending on the learning rate, with the best configuration reaching a mean ratio of 5.08$\times$. Imperceptible perturbations ($\varepsilon=0.01$) also reliably increase entropy above the baseline.
L117: This shows that significant decoding instability can be induced without visible image degradation, though the effect is less severe than unconstrained attacks.
L118: For the black-box scenario (Panel B), the best unconstrained configuration reaches a mean ratio of 1.65$\times$, showing that the perturbation transfers uncertainty also to unseen models. Lower budgets reduce transfer, with ratios near 1.1$\times$. Panel C demonstrates the efficacy of the white-box patch attack. Constraining the perturbation to a $224\times 224$ region yields a mean ratio of 3.05$\times$.
L119: This shows that a patch can disrupt models’ decoding by modifying only $\approx 9\%$ of the image pixels.
L120: Proprietary evaluations in Table cite28†4 follow a similar trend. At $\varepsilon=1.0$, GPT-5.1, GPT-o3, GPT-4o, and Nova Pro produce coherent hallucinations, while Grok 4 issues a safety refusal (Table cite29†1 ). Lower-budget perturbations fail to transfer and result in accurate descriptions of the original website. High-entropy perturbations therefore generalize beyond the training ensemble, but basic PGD fails to produce transferable perturbations under small-budget constraints.

L128: ## 4 Discussion
L129: Confusion Modes. We categorize the observed adversarial effects into five distinct modes: Blindness, where the model claims inability to view or process the image; Subtle, where the model describes the high-level domain of the image but generates incorrect or uninformative text; Language Switch, characterized by unprompted shifts to non-English scripts; Delusional, involving confident hallucinations of nonexistent objects; and Collapse, a complete breakdown of semantic coherence marked by repetition loops.
L130: In the white-box setting, we observed the full spectrum of confusion modes. Collapse was typically associated with peak entropy values, whereas Subtle and Delusional modes correlated with lower entropy increases. In the black-box transfer to proprietary models, Collapse and Blindness were absent; instead, these models exhibited primarily Delusional hallucinations and Language Switch.
L131: Imperceptibility. In our setting, $\varepsilon=0.01$ perturbations are visually imperceptible, but they fail to transfer. Consistent with prior work [cite22†8 , cite23†9 , cite24†10 , cite15†1 , cite21†7 ], simple PGD-style attacks show limited transferability under very small budgets. However, in some practical settings, visual imperceptibility is a preference rather than a requirement. For adversarial patches designed to block AI Agents from operating on websites, the primary goal is Denial of Service.
L132: A visible, high-entropy noise patch ($\varepsilon=1.0$) that reliably induces agent malfunction is therefore a reasonable defense mechanism, even if the perturbation is conspicuous to human users.
L133: Limitations & Future Work. This study uses an entropy-maximization objective implemented with PGD, a basic first-order adversarial optimization technique. Future work should investigate whether feature-level disruptions or more advanced momentum-based adversarial methods [cite23†9 ] can help bridge the entropy gap between white-box and black-box settings. Enhancing robustness to compression, rendering, and small geometric transformations is also important for real-world deployment [cite30†11 ].
L134: The adversarial confusion attack also warrants evaluation within complex, multi-step agentic workflows [cite31†12 ]. A particularly interesting direction is exploring how adversarial confusion can be embedded into website design, such as through background textures or UI color schemes.
L135: ## 5 Conclusion
L136: We introduced the Adversarial Confusion Attack, a method for disrupting Multimodal Large Language Models by maximizing next-token entropy. Using a standard Projected Gradient Descent optimizer and a small surrogate ensemble, we showed that a single perturbation—applied globally or as a localized patch—can reliably destabilize model decoding.
L137: The attack transfers to unseen open-source and proprietary models in the full-image setting, indicating that entropy-based perturbations exploit vulnerabilities shared across current MLLMs [cite32†13 ]. These results position confusion attacks as a novel defense against unauthorized AI Agent activity, deployable via the proposed Adversarial CAPTCHA or, in future applications, through direct integration into website UIs.
